Apple's FY2025 10-K discloses two dedicated supply chain risk factors in Item 1A — dependence on outsourced manufacturing/logistics partners and the ability to obtain components in sufficient quantities — supplemented by related trade-restriction and business-interruption risks.

**1. Dependence on outsourcing partners for manufacturing and logistics (p.10)**
- A significant majority of Apple's manufacturing is performed by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, plus sourcing from U.S. partners and facilities; it relies on single-source partners in the U.S., Asia and Europe for many components and on partners primarily in Asia for final assembly of substantially all hardware products, and has outsourced much of its transportation and logistics management.
- These arrangements lower operating costs but reduce Apple's direct control over production and distribution, which has from time to time adversely affected the cost, quality or quantity of products and its flexibility to respond to changing conditions.
- Apple generally remains responsible to consumers for warranty and out-of-warranty service despite defect-reimbursement provisions, and experiences unanticipated product defect liabilities; supplier code of conduct violations occur from time to time and can materially adversely affect the business.
- Changes or additions to the supply chain require considerable time and resources and carry significant risks and uncertainties, including additional regulatory and operational risks.

**2. Obtaining components in sufficient quantities on commercially reasonable terms (pp.10–11)**
- Certain components come from single or limited sources, exposing Apple to significant supply and pricing risks; even multi-source components are at times subject to industry-wide shortages and commodity price fluctuations — the filing cites past global semiconductor shortages as an example that could recur.
- New products often use custom components available from only one source, with initial capacity constraints until suppliers' yields mature; Apple may not be able to extend or renew supply agreements on similar terms, or at all, or find alternative sources.
- Component suppliers may fail, consolidate, or shift to producing common components instead of Apple-customized ones, leaving Apple exposed to supply shortages and price increases.

**Related supply chain risks disclosed elsewhere in Item 1A**
- Trade restrictions and tariffs (p.8): beginning in Q2 2025, new U.S. tariffs were announced on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU, with reciprocal/retaliatory measures threatened and a Section 232 investigation into semiconductor imports underway; such measures can raise costs or limit availability of products, components, rare earths and other raw materials, and may force Apple to change suppliers and restructure operations. The filing also notes global supply chains are highly concentrated and that escalating geopolitical tensions or conflict could cause significant disruptions.
- Business interruptions (p.8): political events, trade disputes, geopolitical tensions, conflict, terrorism, natural disasters, public health issues and industrial accidents can materially adversely affect Apple's suppliers, contract manufacturers and logistics providers.
- Margin pressure (p.17): supply shortages and potential increases in the cost of components and outside manufacturing services are listed among factors pressuring net sales and gross margins.

Sources: [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.10], [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.11], [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.8], [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.17]

In its FY2025 10-K (fiscal year ended June 30, 2025), Microsoft reports three segments — **Productivity and Business Processes ($120.8 billion revenue), Intelligent Cloud ($106.3 billion), and More Personal Computing ($54.6 billion)** — which together sum to Microsoft's $281.7 billion consolidated revenue. The August 2024 change most notably brought the commercial components of Microsoft 365 together in the Productivity and Business Processes segment, and prior-period segment information was recast to conform.

**Segment definitions and FY2025 revenue:**

- **Productivity and Business Processes — $120.8 billion.** Products and services in the portfolio of productivity, communication, and information services, spanning a variety of devices and platforms. Primarily comprises: (1) Microsoft 365 Commercial products and cloud services, including Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud (Microsoft 365 Commercial, Enterprise Mobility + Security, the cloud portion of Windows Commercial, the per-user portion of Power BI, Exchange, SharePoint, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft 365 Security and Compliance, and Microsoft 365 Copilot) and Microsoft 365 Commercial products (Windows Commercial on-premises and Office licensed on-premises); (2) Microsoft 365 Consumer products and cloud services; (3) LinkedIn (Talent, Marketing, Premium Subscriptions, and Sales Solutions); and (4) Dynamics products and cloud services, including Dynamics 365 (ERP, CRM, Power Apps, Power Automate) and on-premises ERP/CRM.
- **Intelligent Cloud — $106.3 billion.** Public, private, and hybrid server products and cloud services that power modern business and developers. Primarily comprises: (1) Server products and cloud services, including Azure and other cloud services (cloud and AI consumption-based services, GitHub cloud services, Nuance Healthcare cloud services, virtual desktop offerings, and other cloud services) and server products (SQL Server, Windows Server, Visual Studio, System Center, related CALs, and other on-premises offerings); and (2) Enterprise and partner services (Enterprise Support Services, Industry Solutions, Nuance professional services, Microsoft Partner Network, and Learning Experience).
- **More Personal Computing — $54.6 billion.** Products and services that put customers at the center of the experience with Microsoft's technology. Primarily comprises: (1) Windows and Devices, including Windows OEM licensing (Windows Pro and non-Pro licenses sold through the OEM channel) and Devices (Surface and PC accessories); (2) Gaming, including Xbox hardware and Xbox content and services (first- and third-party content, Xbox Game Pass and other subscriptions, Xbox Cloud Gaming, advertising, and other cloud services); and (3) Search and news advertising (Bing and Copilot, Microsoft News, Microsoft Edge, and third-party affiliates).

For context, the recast FY2024 comparatives under the new definitions were $106.8 billion (Productivity and Business Processes), $87.5 billion (Intelligent Cloud), and $50.8 billion (More Personal Computing); Intelligent Cloud grew 21.5% year over year.

answer:
Microsoft's FY2025 10-K discloses AI-related risks throughout Item 1A (Risk Factors), anchored by a dedicated risk factor titled "Issues in the development, deployment, and use of AI may result in reputational or competitive harm or liability," plus AI-specific mentions in its competition, execution, security, IP, regulatory, and reputation risk factors.

- **Development and deployment flaws (p.23, dedicated risk factor):** AI algorithms or training methodologies may be flawed; datasets may be overbroad, insufficient, or contain biased or inaccurate information; AI-generated content may be offensive, illegal, inaccurate, or otherwise harmful. Inadequate practices by Microsoft or others (including strategic partner OpenAI) could cause incidents that impair acceptance of AI solutions or harm individuals, customers, or society. Human review of inputs/outputs may be required, including for agentic AI systems that act autonomously. These risks stem from intellectual property, data privacy, and other claims tied to AI training and outputs, compounded by an evolving regulatory landscape (including new EU laws), ethical issues, and rising global divergence in how to address them.

- **Competition and execution (p.17):** AI is a "highly competitive and rapidly evolving market" with new competitors continually entering; Microsoft will bear significant development and operational costs to build AI models, services, platforms, and infrastructure. Its focus on cloud-based and AI services presents execution risks — significant infrastructure costs are reducing operating margins, and it is uncertain whether strategies will attract users or generate revenue in line with those investments. Competitors also distribute open AI models at little or no cost without bearing full R&D costs.

- **Misuse and abuse (pp.18, 22):** AI systems may be used in unintended or inappropriate ways, and users may engage in fraudulent or abusive activities through cloud-based and AI services (unauthorized account access, payment fraud, terms-of-service violations including cryptocurrency mining or launching cyberattacks); detection efforts may not be effective. Users may also impersonate people or organizations through AI technologies and disseminate misleading content.

- **Investment returns (p.18):** Significant investments in AI-based products and services may not achieve expected returns — investments in new technology are speculative, may not be profitable, and may not achieve historical operating margins.

- **Security (pp.19–20):** Threat actors may use AI and machine learning in attacks; increasing use of generative AI models in Microsoft's internal systems may create new attack surfaces or methods for adversaries; and features relying on generative AI can be susceptible to security threats.

- **Customer deployment and data practices (p.22):** Customers control Microsoft's AI products within their environments and may deploy them in high-risk scenarios or use them inappropriately; products may collect large amounts of data in ways that don't satisfy customer or regulatory requirements, exposing Microsoft to legal claims or enforcement actions.

- **Intellectual property (p.27):** Third parties may claim infringement, "including current copyright infringement and other claims arising from AI training and output," which could force royalty-bearing data access or licensing agreements, product redesigns, or damages payments under indemnification commitments.

- **Regulation (p.24):** Emerging AI legislation and regulation could increase costs or restrict opportunity — for example, the EU's AI Act may increase costs or impact the provision or operation of Microsoft's AI models and services in the European market. Regulatory areas include model and system development and deployment, frontier model safety, transparency, and content provenance.

- **Reputation (p.27):** Public scrutiny of Microsoft's decisions regarding the development and deployment of AI, and responsible AI failures, are cited among events that could damage its brands and reputation.

Sources: [MSFT FY2025 10-K, pp.17–18, 19–20, 22, 23, 24, 27]

Microsoft's operating income grew by $19.1 billion (+17.4%, from $109.4 billion to $128.5 billion) and Alphabet's by $16.6 billion (+14.8%, from $112.4 billion to $129.0 billion) in their respective fiscal 2025 years. Note the periods differ: Microsoft's FY2025 ended June 30, 2025, while Alphabet's ended December 31, 2025.

**Microsoft — $19.1 billion increase (17.4%)**
- The FY2025 10-K states: "Operating income increased $19.1 billion or 17% with growth across each of our segments" (segment figures below are under the definitions restated after the August 2024 reorganization).
- Productivity and Business Processes: +$10.1 billion (+17%), the largest contributor — revenue up $14.0 billion (+13%) and gross margin up $11.2 billion (+13%), both driven by growth in Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud; operating expenses rose only $1.1 billion (+4%) on cloud/AI engineering and commercial sales investments.
- Intelligent Cloud: +$6.8 billion (+18%) — revenue up $18.8 billion (+21%) driven by Azure and other cloud services (Azure grew 34% on demand for the services portfolio); gross margin percentage declined as AI infrastructure scaling costs outpaced Azure efficiency gains.
- More Personal Computing: +$2.2 billion (+18%) — revenue up $3.8 billion (+7%), led by Gaming (+$2.0 billion, +9%, on Xbox content and services including the Activision Blizzard impact and Game Pass) and Search and news advertising (+$1.6 billion, +13%).

**Alphabet — $16.6 billion increase (14.8%)**
- Google Services: operating income up $18.1 billion (to $139.4 billion), "primarily driven by an increase in revenues, partially offset by an increase in expenses related to legal and other matters, TAC, and content acquisition costs."
- Google Cloud: operating income up $7.8 billion (to $13.9 billion), "primarily driven by an increase in revenues, partially offset by increases in usage costs for technical infrastructure and employee compensation expenses."
- These gains were partly offset by Other Bets' operating loss widening $3.1 billion (to $7.5 billion), driven by employee compensation expense largely from a valuation-based compensation charge related to Waymo, and the Alphabet-level activities loss widening $6.2 billion (to $16.8 billion); consolidated operating expenses rose 22% on employee compensation, legal and other matters, and depreciation.
- Consolidated operating margin held at 32% despite revenue growing 15%.

Both 10-Ks describe AI infrastructure spending as a meaningful driver of rising costs and margin pressure, but with efficiency offsets — Microsoft says scaling its AI infrastructure "will continue to increase our operating costs and may decrease our operating margins" and already cut its gross margin percentage slightly in FY2025, while Alphabet says the costs of operating its AI-scaled technical infrastructure (depreciation, energy, equipment, network capacity) "are expected to significantly increase" and may pressure operating margins going forward. (Note: Microsoft's FY2025 ended June 30, 2025; Alphabet's ended December 31, 2025.)

**Microsoft (FY2025 10-K)**
- MD&A trends (p.34): investments in cloud and AI infrastructure "will continue to increase our operating costs and may decrease our operating margins," as it expands datacenter locations and server capacity (including GPUs) to meet growing AI demand; the Risk Factors section (p.17) repeats that it is "incurring significant costs to build and maintain infrastructure to support cloud-based and AI services, reducing operating margins."
- Realized effect in FY2025 (p.37): cost of revenue rose $13.7 billion or 19% driven by Microsoft Cloud; gross margin percentage "decreased slightly driven by Intelligent Cloud," and Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage fell to 69% "driven by the impact of scaling our AI infrastructure, offset in part by efficiency gains in Azure." In Intelligent Cloud specifically (p.38), cost of revenue rose $10.6 billion or 36% on Azure growth, with gross margin percentage down for the same reason.
- Offsets: efficiency gains in Azure and Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud partially mitigated the AI-infrastructure drag; per the database, gross margin still slipped from 69.8% to 68.8% while operating margin actually rose from 44.6% to 45.6% (operating expenses grew only 4%).

**Alphabet (FY2025 10-K)**
- MD&A "Trends in Our Business and Financial Effect" (p.30): under "Increased Investment in Technical Infrastructure," it invested heavily in capex in 2025 and expects to significantly increase investment in 2026 (servers, network equipment, data centers); operating costs — depreciation, energy, equipment, and network capacity — "are expected to significantly increase as developing and serving AI offerings require more compute power than our historical consumer and enterprise offerings." It also cautions (same section) that AI offerings "may monetize differently" than historical offerings, affecting revenue growth and margin trends.
- Offsets: it expects to "continue to drive efficiencies in our data centers, for example, through the design of our AI models and our TPU and GPU-based technical infrastructure."
- Risk Factors (p.12): flags possible "downward pressure on our operating margin" from, among other factors, "a higher level of investment in technical infrastructure."
- Realized effect so far is milder than the warning: per the database, cost of revenue grew 11.1% ($146.3 billion to $162.5 billion), slower than revenue, so cost of revenue as a share of revenue actually fell from 41.8% to 40.3%, and operating margin was roughly flat (32.1% to 32.0%).

**Common framing:** both companies attribute rising cost of revenue to the AI buildout (Microsoft: "scaling our AI infrastructure"; Alphabet: technical-infrastructure costs requiring more compute power), both explicitly warn of margin pressure, and both cite efficiency programs (Azure/Microsoft 365 efficiencies; data-center and TPU/GPU design efficiencies) as partial offsets.

Apple's FY2025 10-K (Item 1A, Risk Factors) discloses two dedicated supply-chain risk factors — dependence on outsourced manufacturing/logistics and the ability to obtain components in sufficient quantities — plus several related risks around trade restrictions, business interruptions, and inventory/purchase commitments.

**Primary supply-chain risk factors:**

- **Dependence on outsourcing partners for manufacturing and logistics (p.10):** A significant majority of Apple's manufacturing is performed by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam (plus U.S. partners/facilities). Apple relies on single-source partners in the U.S., Asia and Europe for many components, and on partners primarily in Asia for final assembly of substantially all hardware products, and has outsourced much of its transportation and logistics management. These arrangements reduce Apple's direct control over production and distribution, have at times adversely affected cost, quality or quantity, leave Apple responsible for warranty service on defects, and expose it to supplier code-of-conduct violations. Changes or additions to the supply chain require considerable time and resources and carry additional regulatory and operational risks.

- **Obtaining components in sufficient quantities on commercially reasonable terms (pp.10–11):** Because Apple obtains certain components from single or limited sources, it faces significant supply and pricing risks, including industrywide shortages and commodity price fluctuations — citing past global semiconductor shortages that impaired its ability to obtain components. New products often use custom components available from only one source, with initial capacity constraints until supplier yields mature; Apple may not be able to extend or renew supply agreements, and suppliers may fail, consolidate, or shift to producing common components instead of Apple's custom ones.

- **Trade restrictions, tariffs and geopolitical tensions (pp.8–9):** Restrictions on international trade (tariffs and import/export controls) can materially adversely affect Apple's supply chain — particularly where it has significant supply-chain operations. The filing specifically notes that beginning in Q2 2025, new U.S. tariffs were announced on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU, with retaliatory measures threatened, and a Section 232 investigation into semiconductor imports. It warns that global supply chains are highly concentrated and that escalating geopolitical tensions or conflict could cause significant disruptions; restrictive measures can raise costs, limit availability of components and rare earths, and force supplier changes that are expensive and time-consuming.

- **Business interruptions (p.9):** Natural disasters (many supplier and contract-manufacturer operations are in earthquake-prone locations), fires, power shortages, industrial accidents, labor disputes, public health issues and other events can create delays and inefficiencies in the supply and manufacturing chain. Because Apple relies on single or limited sources for many critical components, a business interruption affecting those sources would exacerbate the consequences, and insurance may be insufficient.

- **Inventory write-downs and purchase-commitment risk (p.11):** Apple orders components and builds inventory in advance of product announcements, with manufacturing purchase obligations typically covering up to 150 days of forecasted requirements; volatile markets create the risk of ordering excess or insufficient components or not fully utilizing purchase commitments, with cancellation fee reserves accrued for excess orders.

- **Related risks (pp.13–14):** Apple and its global supply chain depend on complex IT systems whose failure could impede manufacturing and shipping, and Apple's suppliers are themselves exposed to ransomware and other malicious attacks that can disrupt operations.

Both companies' FY2025 10-Ks describe AI infrastructure buildout as a meaningful driver of rising costs and margin pressure — Microsoft quantifies it as a slight gross-margin decline from "scaling our AI infrastructure," while Alphabet frames it as technical-infrastructure costs that are "expected to significantly increase," pressuring operating margins going forward. (Note: Microsoft's FY2025 ended June 30, 2025; Alphabet's ended December 31, 2025.)

**Microsoft (FY2025 10-K)**
- MD&A: FY2025 cost of revenue rose $13.7 billion or 19% (database: +18.5%, $74.1B → $87.8B), driven by growth in Microsoft Cloud, and gross margin percentage "decreased slightly" (database: 69.8% → 68.8%). Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage fell to 69% "driven by the impact of scaling our AI infrastructure, offset in part by efficiency gains in Azure" (p.37).

Despite this, operating margin actually rose from 44.6% to 45.6% (database).

**Alphabet (FY2025 10-K)**
- MD&A "Trends": costs of operating technical infrastructure — "depreciation, energy, equipment, and network capacity — are expected to significantly increase as developing and serving AI offerings require more compute power than our historical consumer and enterprise offerings," while Alphabet expects to keep driving data-center efficiencies through AI model design and its TPU/GPU-based infrastructure (p.30).

Both companies' FY2025 10-Ks say AI infrastructure buildout is raising their costs and pressuring margins, but Microsoft frames it as an effect already visible in FY2025 results (gross margin percentage down slightly), while Alphabet frames it mainly as a forward-looking trend (operating costs expected to "significantly increase" as AI capex ramps).

**Microsoft (FY2025 10-K, fiscal year ended June 30, 2025)**
- MD&A states directly: "The investments we are making in cloud and AI infrastructure and devices will continue to increase our operating costs and may decrease our operating margins" (p.34), citing datacenter expansion to meet "growing demand for AI services" and dependence on land, energy, networking supplies, and GPUs. The Risk Factors echo this: "We are incurring significant costs to build and maintain infrastructure to support cloud-based and AI services, reducing operating margins" (p.17).
- In the FY2025 vs. FY2024 results, cost of revenue rose $13.7 billion or 19% driven by growth in Microsoft Cloud, and gross margin percentage "decreased slightly driven by Intelligent Cloud" (p.37). Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage fell to 69% "driven by the impact of scaling our AI infrastructure, offset in part by efficiency gains in Azure" (p.37).
- At the segment level, Intelligent Cloud cost of revenue rose $10.6 billion or 36% driven by Azure, with gross margin percentage down from scaling AI infrastructure, partly offset by Azure efficiency gains; Productivity and Business Processes saw a similar slight decline from AI infrastructure scaling (p.38).
- Database figures confirm the pattern: cost of revenue rose 18.5% to $87.8 billion, gross margin fell from 69.8% to 68.8%, while operating margin actually rose from 44.6% to 45.6% on revenue growth of 15%.

**Alphabet (FY2025 10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025)**
- The MD&A "Trends in Our Business and Financial Effect" section (p.30) says Alphabet invested heavily in capital expenditures in 2025 and expects to "significantly increase" investment in 2026 in servers, network equipment, and data centers, and that the costs of operating its technical infrastructure — "depreciation, energy, equipment, and network capacity — are expected to significantly increase as developing and serving AI offerings require more compute power than our historical consumer and enterprise offerings." It adds a partial offset: it expects to "continue to drive efficiencies in our data centers, for example, through the design of our AI models and our TPU and GPU-based technical infrastructure."
- The same section notes AI offerings (AI Overviews, AI Mode in Search, enterprise AI on Google Cloud) "may monetize differently than our historical consumer and enterprise offerings which could affect revenue growth rates and margin trends" (p.30).
- Risk Factors warn of "downward pressure on our operating margin" from "a higher level of investment in technical infrastructure," plus margin compression from a growing mix of lower-margin businesses such as Google Cloud and devices (p.12).
- Database figures show the realized effect so far: cost of revenue rose 11.1% to $162.5 billion, gross margin actually improved from 58.2% to 59.7%, and operating margin was roughly flat (32.0% vs. 32.1%) — consistent with Alphabet presenting the cost pressure as prospective rather than already depressing margins.

Apple's FY2025 10-K discloses two dedicated supply chain risk factors in Item 1A — dependence on outsourced manufacturing/logistics partners and the ability to obtain components in sufficient quantities — supplemented by related trade-restriction and business-interruption risks.

**1. Dependence on outsourcing partners for manufacturing and logistics (p.10)**
- A significant majority of Apple's manufacturing is performed by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, plus sourcing from U.S. partners and facilities; it relies on single-source partners in the U.S., Asia and Europe for many components and on partners primarily in Asia for final assembly of substantially all hardware products, and has outsourced much of its transportation and logistics management.
- These arrangements lower operating costs but reduce Apple's direct control over production and distribution, which has from time to time adversely affected the cost, quality or quantity of products and its flexibility to respond to changing conditions.
- Apple generally remains responsible to consumers for warranty and out-of-warranty service despite defect-reimbursement provisions, and experiences unanticipated product defect liabilities; supplier code of conduct violations occur from time to time and can materially adversely affect the business.
- Changes or additions to the supply chain require considerable time and resources and carry significant risks and uncertainties, including additional regulatory and operational risks.

**2. Obtaining components in sufficient quantities on commercially reasonable terms (pp.10–11)**
- Certain components come from single or limited sources, exposing Apple to significant supply and pricing risks; even multi-source components are at times subject to industry-wide shortages and commodity price fluctuations — the filing cites past global semiconductor shortages as an example that could recur.
- New products often use custom components available from only one source, with initial capacity constraints until suppliers' yields mature; Apple may not be able to extend or renew supply agreements on similar terms, or at all, or find alternative sources.
- Component suppliers may fail, consolidate, or shift to producing common components instead of Apple-customized ones, leaving Apple exposed to supply shortages and price increases.

**Related supply chain risks disclosed elsewhere in Item 1A**
- Trade restrictions and tariffs (p.8): beginning in Q2 2025, new U.S. tariffs were announced on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU, with reciprocal/retaliatory measures threatened and a Section 232 investigation into semiconductor imports underway; such measures can raise costs or limit availability of products, components, rare earths and other raw materials, and may force Apple to change suppliers and restructure operations. The filing also notes global supply chains are highly concentrated and that escalating geopolitical tensions or conflict could cause significant disruptions.
- Business interruptions (p.8): political events, trade disputes, geopolitical tensions, conflict, terrorism, natural disasters, public health issues and industrial accidents can materially adversely affect Apple's suppliers, contract manufacturers and logistics providers.
- Margin pressure (p.17): supply shortages and potential increases in the cost of components and outside manufacturing services are listed among factors pressuring net sales and gross margins.

answer:
Microsoft's FY2025 10-K discloses AI-related risks throughout Item 1A (Risk Factors), anchored by a dedicated risk factor titled "Issues in the development, deployment, and use of AI may result in reputational or competitive harm or liability," plus AI-specific mentions in its competition, execution, security, IP, regulatory, and reputation risk factors.

- **Development and deployment flaws (p.23, dedicated risk factor):** AI algorithms or training methodologies may be flawed; datasets may be overbroad, insufficient, or contain biased or inaccurate information; AI-generated content may be offensive, illegal, inaccurate, or otherwise harmful. Inadequate practices by Microsoft or others (including strategic partner OpenAI) could cause incidents that impair acceptance of AI solutions or harm individuals, customers, or society. Human review of inputs/outputs may be required, including for agentic AI systems that act autonomously. These risks stem from intellectual property, data privacy, and other claims tied to AI training and outputs, compounded by an evolving regulatory landscape (including new EU laws), ethical issues, and rising global divergence in how to address them.

- **Competition and execution (p.17):** AI is a "highly competitive and rapidly evolving market" with new competitors continually entering; Microsoft will bear significant development and operational costs to build AI models, services, platforms, and infrastructure. Its focus on cloud-based and AI services presents execution risks — significant infrastructure costs are reducing operating margins, and it is uncertain whether strategies will attract users or generate revenue in line with those investments. Competitors also distribute open AI models at little or no cost without bearing full R&D costs.

- **Misuse and abuse (pp.18, 22):** AI systems may be used in unintended or inappropriate ways, and users may engage in fraudulent or abusive activities through cloud-based and AI services (unauthorized account access, payment fraud, terms-of-service violations including cryptocurrency mining or launching cyberattacks); detection efforts may not be effective. Users may also impersonate people or organizations through AI technologies and disseminate misleading content.

- **Investment returns (p.18):** Significant investments in AI-based products and services may not achieve expected returns — investments in new technology are speculative, may not be profitable, and may not achieve historical operating margins.

- **Security (pp.19–20):** Threat actors may use AI and machine learning in attacks; increasing use of generative AI models in Microsoft's internal systems may create new attack surfaces or methods for adversaries; and features relying on generative AI can be susceptible to security threats.

- **Customer deployment and data practices (p.22):** Customers control Microsoft's AI products within their environments and may deploy them in high-risk scenarios or use them inappropriately; products may collect large amounts of data in ways that don't satisfy customer or regulatory requirements, exposing Microsoft to legal claims or enforcement actions.

- **Intellectual property (p.27):** Third parties may claim infringement, "including current copyright infringement and other claims arising from AI training and output," which could force royalty-bearing data access or licensing agreements, product redesigns, or damages payments under indemnification commitments.

- **Regulation (p.24):** Emerging AI legislation and regulation could increase costs or restrict opportunity — for example, the EU's AI Act may increase costs or impact the provision or operation of Microsoft's AI models and services in the European market. Regulatory areas include model and system development and deployment, frontier model safety, transparency, and content provenance.

- **Reputation (p.27):** Public scrutiny of Microsoft's decisions regarding the development and deployment of AI, and responsible AI failures, are cited among events that could damage its brands and reputation.

In its FY2025 Form 10-K (Item 1A, Risk Factors), Apple's primary supply chain risk factors were its dependence on outsourced manufacturing concentrated in Asia, its reliance on single- or limited-source component suppliers, and its exposure to trade restrictions/tariffs and business interruptions.

- **Dependence on outsourcing partners (p.10):** A significant majority of Apple's manufacturing is performed by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam; it relies on single-source partners in the U.S., Asia and Europe for many components and on partners primarily in Asia for final assembly of substantially all hardware products, and has outsourced much of its transportation and logistics management. This reduces direct control over production and distribution (affecting cost, quality, quantity and flexibility), leaves Apple responsible for warranty service on defects, exposes it to supplier code-of-conduct violations, and means changes or additions to the supply chain require considerable time and resources and carry additional regulatory and operational risks.

- **Obtaining components in sufficient quantities on commercially reasonable terms (p.10–11):** Certain components come from single or limited sources, exposing Apple to supply and pricing risks; even multi-source components face industrywide shortages and commodity price fluctuations (e.g., past global semiconductor shortages). New products often use custom components available from only one source with initial capacity constraints; Apple may be unable to extend or renew supply agreements, and suppliers may fail, consolidate, or shift to producing common components instead — leaving Apple subject to significant risks of supply shortages and price increases.

- **Trade restrictions and tariffs (p.8):** Beginning in the second quarter of 2025, new U.S. tariffs were announced on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU, with several countries imposing or threatening reciprocal tariffs; the U.S. Commerce Department also initiated a Section 232 investigation into semiconductor imports. Such restrictions can increase costs or limit availability of products, components, rare earths and other raw materials, and may force Apple to change suppliers and restructure operations — which is expensive, time-consuming and disruptive. Apple notes global supply chains are highly concentrated and that escalating geopolitical tensions or conflict could cause significant disruptions.

- **Business interruptions (p.8–9):** Apple's operations and its suppliers' and contract manufacturers' facilities are in locations prone to earthquakes and other natural disasters (intensified by climate change), plus fire, power shortages, industrial accidents, terrorism, ransomware, labor disputes and public health issues. Because Apple relies on single or limited sources for many critical components, an interruption affecting those sources would exacerbate the consequences, and insurance coverage may be insufficient.

- **Inventory write-downs and purchase commitment risk (p.11):** Apple orders components and builds inventory in advance of product announcements, with manufacturing purchase obligations typically covering up to 150 days; volatile markets create the risk of forecasting incorrectly and ordering excess or insufficient components, leading to write-downs and cancellation fee reserves.

- **Related risks (p.11, p.13):** Defects in components purchased from third parties could make products unsafe and trigger recalls, warranty expenses and product liability claims; and Apple's global supply chain depends on complex IT systems whose failure — or ransomware attacks on its global suppliers — can impede the manufacturing and shipping of its products.

Microsoft's FY2025 10-K discloses AI-related risks throughout Item 1A (Risk Factors), anchored by a dedicated risk factor — "Issues in the development, deployment, and use of AI may result in reputational or competitive harm or liability" — plus AI-specific mentions in its competition, execution, security, misuse, IP, regulatory, and reputation risk factors. The main disclosures are:

- **Development and deployment flaws (p.23):** AI algorithms or training methodologies may be flawed; datasets may be overbroad, insufficient, or contain biased or inaccurate information; AI-generated content may be offensive, illegal, inaccurate, or otherwise harmful. Inadequate practices by Microsoft or others (including strategic partner OpenAI) could cause incidents that impair acceptance of AI solutions or harm individuals, customers, or society. Human review of inputs/outputs may be required, including for agentic AI systems that act autonomously. Risks stem from intellectual property, data privacy, and other claims tied to AI training and outputs, compounded by an evolving regulatory landscape (including new EU laws), ethical issues, and divergent global approaches Microsoft must navigate across geographies.

- **Legal and regulatory risk (p.24):** Emerging AI legislation and regulation could increase costs or restrict opportunity — for example, the EU's AI Act may increase costs or impact the provision or operation of Microsoft's AI models and services in the European market. Regulatory areas cited include model and system development and deployment, frontier model safety, transparency, and content provenance. Separately (p.27), third parties may claim infringement from AI training and output, potentially forcing royalty-bearing data access or licensing agreements, product redesign, or damages payments under indemnification commitments.

- **Competition and execution risk (p.17):** AI is a "highly competitive and rapidly evolving market" with new entrants, and Microsoft will bear significant development and operational costs to build AI models, services, platforms, and infrastructure. Its focus on cloud-based and AI services presents execution risks — infrastructure spending is reducing operating margins, and success depends on execution in bringing compelling services to market, maintaining performance across devices, attracting developers, and meeting reliability/security/compliance needs; it is uncertain whether strategies will generate revenue in line with these investments. Competitors also distribute open AI models at little or no cost without bearing full R&D costs.

- **Investment risk (p.18):** Significant investments in AI-based products and services may not achieve expected returns — investments in new technology are speculative, revenue may take years, and margins may be lower than historical levels.

- **Misuse and abuse (p.18, p.22):** AI systems may be used in unintended or inappropriate ways; users may engage in fraudulent or abusive activities through cloud-based and AI services (unauthorized account access, payment fraud, terms-of-service violations including cryptocurrency mining or launching cyberattacks), and Microsoft's detection efforts may not be effective. Users may also impersonate people or organizations through AI technologies on its platforms, and customers may deploy Microsoft's AI products in high-risk scenarios or use them inappropriately within their own environments.

- **Security and reputational risk (p.19–20, p.27):** Threat actors may use AI and machine learning in attacks; increasing use of generative AI in Microsoft's internal systems may create new attack surfaces; and features relying on generative AI can be susceptible to security threats. Reputationally, Microsoft cites public scrutiny of its decisions on AI development and deployment, and "responsible AI failures," as potential sources of brand damage.

Microsoft's FY2025 10-K discloses AI-related risks across its competition, execution, security, product-liability, intellectual property, regulatory, and reputational risk factors, with a dedicated AI risk factor in Item 1A.

- **Competition (p.17):** AI technology and services are a highly competitive, rapidly evolving market with new competitors continually entering; Microsoft will bear significant development and operational costs to build and support AI models, services, platforms, and infrastructure, and must stay responsive to technological change, regulatory developments, and public scrutiny; separately, some competitors distribute open source software and open AI models at little or no cost without bearing full R&D costs, mimicking Microsoft's features.
- **Execution risk of cloud-based and AI services (p.17):** Significant infrastructure costs to support cloud and AI services are reducing operating margins; success depends on execution — bringing compelling AI services to market, maintaining their utility/compatibility/performance across devices, attracting third-party developers, meeting reliability, security, and compliance requirements, and staying platform-agnostic — and it is uncertain the strategies will attract users or generate revenue in line with these investments.
- **Misuse of AI systems (p.18):** AI systems may be used in unintended or inappropriate ways, and users may engage in fraudulent or abusive activities through cloud-based and AI services (unauthorized account access, payment fraud, terms-of-service violations including cryptocurrency mining or launching cyberattacks); Microsoft's detection and control efforts may not be effective, risking reputational damage and adverse business impact.
- **Investment returns (p.18):** Significant investments in AI-based products and services are speculative — revenue may not materialize for several years, if at all; new offerings may not be profitable or achieve historical operating margins, and data-handling practices will remain under scrutiny.
- **Acquisitions and partnerships (p.18):** The OpenAI strategic partnership (third phase announced January 2023) and other arrangements carry risks including unsatisfactory returns, integration challenges, limited ability to control third parties, and dependence on partners meeting Microsoft's policies on responsible AI, data governance, privacy, digital safety, and cybersecurity.
- **Security (pp.19–20):** Threat actors may use emerging technologies such as AI and machine learning in attacks; increasing use of generative AI models in Microsoft's internal systems may create new attack surfaces or adversary methods; and features that rely on generative AI can be susceptible to security threats.
- **Platform abuse (p.22):** Users may impersonate people or organizations through the use of AI technologies and disseminate misleading or manipulative information on Microsoft's advertising, professional, marketplace, and gaming platforms; preventing this requires substantial investment that may not succeed.
- **Customer deployment and data practices (p.22):** Customers control Microsoft's AI products within their own environments and may deploy them in high-risk scenarios or use them inappropriately, and products may collect large amounts of data in ways that don't satisfy customer or regulatory requirements, exposing Microsoft to legal claims or enforcement actions.
- **Intellectual property (p.27):** Third parties claim Microsoft infringes their IP, including current copyright infringement and other claims arising from AI training and output; outcomes could force royalty-bearing data access or licensing agreements on less favorable terms, product redesigns or sales stops, or damages to satisfy indemnification commitments.
- **Regulation (p.24):** Emerging AI legislation and regulation could increase costs or restrict opportunity — for example, the EU's AI Act may increase costs or impact the provision or operation of Microsoft's AI models and services in the European market — with regulatory focus on model and system development and deployment, frontier model safety, transparency, and content provenance.
- **Reputation and brands (p.27):** Brand damage could result from public scrutiny of Microsoft's decisions regarding the development and deployment of AI and from responsible AI failures, amplified by social media's speed and reach.

In its FY2025 Form 10-K (Item 1A, Risk Factors), Apple's primary supply-chain risk factors were its dependence on outsourced manufacturing and logistics partners concentrated outside the U.S., reliance on single- and limited-source components, exposure to trade restrictions and tariffs, vulnerability to business interruptions, and inventory/purchase-commitment risks.

- **Outsourced manufacturing and logistics (p.10):** a significant majority of manufacturing is performed by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam (plus U.S. sourcing); single-source partners in the U.S., Asia and Europe supply many components, and partners primarily in Asia perform final assembly of substantially all hardware products; much of transportation and logistics management is outsourced, reducing Apple's direct control over production and distribution and adversely affecting cost, quality, quantity and flexibility.
- **Warranty and supplier-conduct exposure (p.10):** Apple generally remains responsible to consumers for warranty and out-of-warranty service for product defects despite reimbursement provisions, and supplier code of conduct violations occur from time to time.
- **Supply-chain changes (p.10):** changes or additions to the supply chain require considerable time and resources and involve significant risks, including additional regulatory and operational risks.
- **Component availability and pricing (p.10–11):** certain components come from single or limited sources, creating significant supply and pricing risks; components face industrywide shortages and commodity price fluctuations (e.g., past global semiconductor shortages); new products often use custom components available from only one source with initial capacity constraints; Apple may be unable to extend or renew supply agreements, and suppliers may fail, consolidate, or shift to common components — leaving Apple exposed to supply shortages and price increases.
- **Trade restrictions and tariffs (p.8):** restrictions on international trade (tariffs, import/export controls) can increase the cost or limit availability of products, components, rare earths and other raw materials, and can force supplier changes and restructuring; new U.S. tariffs announced beginning in Q2 2025 on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU (with threatened reciprocal retaliation), plus a Section 232 investigation into semiconductor imports, create uncertain impacts; global supply chains are highly concentrated, and escalating geopolitical tensions or conflict could cause significant disruptions.
- **Business interruptions (p.8–9):** political events, geopolitical tensions, conflict, terrorism, natural disasters, public health issues and industrial accidents at suppliers and contract manufacturers can make it difficult or impossible to manufacture and deliver products; because Apple relies on single or limited sources for many critical components, an interruption affecting those sources would exacerbate the consequences, and insurance may be insufficient.
- **Inventory write-downs and purchase commitments (p.11):** Apple orders components and builds inventory in advance of announcements and shipments, with manufacturing purchase obligations typically up to 150 days; volatile markets create the risk of forecasting incorrectly and ordering excess or insufficient components, leading to write-downs and cancellation fee reserves.
- **Third-party component defects (p.11):** defects can exist in components purchased from third parties, creating safety, environmental and personal-injury risks and exposing Apple to recalls, warranty expenses and litigation.
- **Supplier IT and cybersecurity (p.13–14):** Apple and its global supply chain depend on complex IT systems whose failure or disruption can impede manufacturing and shipping, and its global suppliers are exposed to ransomware and other malicious attacks that can disrupt business operations.

Apple's FY2025 10-K (Item 1A) discloses two dedicated supply chain risk factors — dependence on outsourced manufacturing and logistics partners, and the ability to obtain components in sufficient quantities on commercially reasonable terms — plus supply chain exposure from trade restrictions/tariffs and business-interruption events.

- **Outsourced manufacturing concentration:** a significant majority of manufacturing is performed by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam (plus U.S. partners/facilities); single-source partners in the U.S., Asia and Europe supply and manufacture many components, and partners primarily in Asia perform final assembly of substantially all hardware products; much of transportation and logistics management is also outsourced (p.10).
- **Diminished control:** these arrangements lower operating costs but reduce direct control over production and distribution, which has from time to time had — and may in the future have — an adverse effect on the cost, quality or quantity of products or on flexibility to respond to changing conditions (p.10).
- **Defect and warranty exposure:** despite provisions for product defect expense reimbursement, Apple generally remains responsible to the consumer for warranty and out-of-warranty service and experiences unanticipated product defect liabilities from time to time (p.10).
- **Supplier conduct:** violations by partners of Apple's supplier code of conduct occur from time to time and can materially adversely affect its business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition and stock price (p.10).
- **Supply chain transition risk:** changes or additions to the supply chain require considerable time and resources and involve significant risks and uncertainties, including exposure to additional regulatory and operational risks (p.10).
- **Single/limited-source components:** certain components come from single or limited sources, creating significant supply and pricing risks; even multi-source components are at times subject to industrywide shortages and significant commodity pricing fluctuations, as with past global semiconductor shortages (pp.10–11).
- **Custom components:** new products often use custom components available from only one source, with initial capacity constraints until supplier yields mature; Apple may not be able to extend or renew supply agreements on similar terms, obtain sufficient quantities in a timely manner, or find alternative sources; suppliers may fail, consolidate, or shift to producing common components instead (p.11).
- **Trade restrictions and tariffs:** tariffs and other import/export controls can materially adversely affect the business and supply chain — raising costs or limiting availability of products, components, rare earths and other raw materials, and potentially forcing supplier changes and restructuring; new U.S. Tariffs announced beginning in Q2 2025 cover imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU, with threatened reciprocal tariffs and a Section 232 investigation into semiconductors and downstream products; such measures can be announced with little or no notice (p.8).
- **Business interruptions:** political events, trade and international disputes, geopolitical tensions, conflict, terrorism, natural disasters, public health issues and industrial accidents can materially adversely affect suppliers, contract manufacturers and logistics providers; global supply chains are highly concentrated, and escalation of geopolitical tensions or conflict could result in significant disruptions (p.8).
- **Margin and regulatory knock-on effects:** supply shortages, potential increases in component and outside manufacturing services costs, and new or increased tariffs are cited as sources of net sales and gross margin volatility (p.17), and new or changing laws and regulations can require changes to Apple's business or supply chain (p.15).

answer:
Microsoft's FY2025 10-K discloses AI-related risks across its competition, execution, security, product-liability, intellectual property, regulatory, and reputational risk factors, with a dedicated AI risk factor in Item 1A.

- **Dedicated AI risk factor (p.23):** "Issues in the development, deployment, and use of AI may result in reputational or competitive harm or liability" — AI algorithms or training methodologies may be flawed; datasets may be overbroad, insufficient, or contain biased or inaccurate information; AI-generated content may be offensive, illegal, inaccurate, or otherwise harmful; inadequate development or deployment practices by Microsoft or others (including strategic partner OpenAI) could cause incidents that impair AI acceptance or harm individuals, customers, or society; human review may be required for agentic AI systems that act autonomously; risks stem from intellectual property, data privacy, and other claims tied to AI training and outputs; ethical issues, broad societal impacts, and divergent global approaches create a "web of different tensions across geographies"; AI solutions with unintended consequences or contrary to responsible AI policies could hurt reputation, competitive position, and results.
- **Competitive risk (p.17):** AI is a highly competitive, rapidly evolving market with new entrants; Microsoft will bear significant development and operational costs to build and support AI models, services, platforms, and infrastructure, and must respond to technological change, regulatory developments, and public scrutiny; competitors also distribute open AI models at little or no cost without bearing full R&D costs.
- **Execution risk (p.17):** Significant infrastructure spending for cloud-based and AI services is reducing operating margins, and success depends on execution (compelling services, device compatibility, developer attractiveness, reliability/security/compliance, platform-agnostic availability); it is uncertain the strategies will attract users or generate revenue in line with these investments.
- **Investment risk (p.18):** Significant investments in AI-based products and services are speculative and may not achieve expected returns or historical margins, with revenue possibly delayed for years.
- **Misuse risk (p.18):** AI systems may be used in unintended or inappropriate ways, and users may commit fraud or abuse through cloud-based and AI services (unauthorized account access, payment fraud, terms-of-service violations including cryptocurrency mining or launching cyberattacks); detection efforts may not be effective.
- **Customer-deployment risk (p.22):** Customers control Microsoft's AI products within their environments and may deploy them in high-risk scenarios or use them inappropriately, and products may collect data in ways that don't satisfy customer or regulatory requirements, exposing Microsoft to legal claims or enforcement.
- **Security risks (pp.19–20):** Threat actors may use AI and machine learning in attacks; increasing internal use of generative AI models may create new attack surfaces; and features relying on generative AI can be susceptible to security threats.
- **Platform abuse (p.22):** Users may impersonate people or organizations through AI technologies and disseminate misleading or manipulative information, requiring substantial and possibly unsuccessful investments to prevent.
- **Intellectual property risk (p.27):** Third parties may claim infringement, including copyright and other claims arising from AI training and output, potentially forcing royalty-bearing data access or licensing agreements, product redesigns, or indemnification payments.
- **Regulatory risk (p.24):** Emerging AI legislation and regulation could increase costs or restrict opportunity — e.g., the EU's AI Act may raise costs or affect provision or operation of AI models and services in Europe — covering model and system development and deployment, frontier model safety, transparency, and content provenance.
- **Reputational risk (p.27):** Public scrutiny of decisions on the development and deployment of AI, and responsible AI failures, are among the events that could damage Microsoft's brands and reputation.
- **Partnership risk (p.18):** The OpenAI strategic partnership (third phase announced January 2023) is cited among acquisitions and alliances whose benefits depend partly on parties meeting Microsoft's policies in areas such as responsible AI, and over which Microsoft has limited control.

Microsoft's FY2025 10-K discloses AI-related risks across Item 1A (Risk Factors), anchored by a dedicated risk factor — "Issues in the development, deployment, and use of AI may result in reputational or competitive harm or liability" — plus AI-specific points woven into its competition, execution, security, IP, regulatory, and reputation risk factors.

- **Development/deployment flaws (dedicated AI risk factor, p.23):** AI algorithms or training methodologies may be flawed; datasets may be overbroad, insufficient, or contain biased or inaccurate information; AI-generated content may be offensive, illegal, inaccurate, or otherwise harmful; inadequate practices by Microsoft or others (including strategic partner OpenAI) could cause incidents that impair acceptance of AI solutions or harm individuals, customers, or society.
- **Agentic AI and human oversight (p.23):** human review of certain inputs and outputs may be required, including for agentic AI systems that can take actions autonomously.
- **Legal exposure from AI (p.23):** implementation of AI systems could result in legal liability, regulatory action, or brand, reputational, or competitive harm, including claims related to intellectual property, data privacy, and AI training and outputs.
- **Ethical and societal issues (p.23):** some AI scenarios present ethical issues or broad societal impacts, with rising global divergence in how to address them, requiring Microsoft to navigate "a web of different tensions across geographies"; AI solutions with unintended consequences, contrary to responsible AI policies, or controversial for impacts on human rights, privacy, employment, or other social, economic, or political issues could hurt reputation, competitive position, and results.
- **Competition (p.17):** AI technology and services are a highly competitive, rapidly evolving market with new entrants; Microsoft will bear significant development and operational costs to build and support AI models, services, platforms, and infrastructure, and must respond to technological change, regulatory developments, and public scrutiny.
- **Open-source AI competitors (p.17):** some companies compete by developing, making available, or using open AI models at little or no cost, monetizing via advertising or integrated products, without bearing full R&D costs, and some open source products mimic Microsoft's features.
- **Execution and margin risk (p.17):** the focus on cloud-based and AI services presents execution and competitive risks — significant infrastructure costs are reducing operating margins, and success depends on execution across compelling offerings, device compatibility, developer attractiveness, reliability/security/compliance, and platform-agnostic availability; revenue may not grow in line with these investments.
- **Investment returns (p.18):** significant investments in AI-based products and services are speculative — revenue may not materialize for several years, if at all, and new offerings may not be profitable or achieve historical operating margins; data-handling practices will remain under scrutiny.
- **Misuse and abuse of AI (p.18):** AI systems may be used in unintended or inappropriate ways, and users may engage in fraudulent or abusive activities through cloud-based and AI services (unauthorized account access, payment fraud, terms-of-service violations including cryptocurrency mining or launching cyberattacks); detection and control efforts may not be effective, risking reputational damage.
- **Customer-controlled deployment (p.22):** customers control Microsoft's AI products within their environments and may deploy them in high-risk scenarios or use them inappropriately, and products may collect large amounts of data in ways that don't satisfy customer or regulatory requirements, exposing Microsoft to legal claims or enforcement actions.
- **Security attack surface (pp.19–20):** threat actors may use AI and machine learning in attacks; increasing use of generative AI models in Microsoft's internal systems may create new attack surfaces or methods for adversaries; and features that rely on generative AI can be susceptible to security threats.
- **AI-enabled impersonation (p.22):** users may impersonate other people or organizations through the use of AI technologies on Microsoft's advertising, professional, marketplace, and gaming platforms, harming reputation or user engagement.
- **IP infringement claims (p.27):** third parties assert copyright infringement and other claims arising from AI training and output; resolutions could include royalty-bearing data access or licensing agreements on less favorable terms, stopping sales or redesigning products, or paying damages under customer indemnification commitments.
- **AI regulation (p.24):** emerging legislative and regulatory action in AI could increase costs or restrict opportunity — for example, the EU's AI Act may increase costs or impact provision or operation of AI models and services in the European market; regulatory focus areas include model and system development and deployment, frontier model safety, transparency, and content provenance.
- **Reputation and brand (p.27):** brand damage could result from public scrutiny of decisions regarding the development and deployment of AI and from responsible AI failures.
- **Partnership/acquisition risk (p.18):** the OpenAI strategic partnership (third phase announced January 2023) is cited among acquisitions and alliances that carry risks, including that acquired or partner companies must meet Microsoft's policies in areas such as responsible AI.

It expects to keep driving datacenter efficiencies through AI model design and its TPU/GPU-based infrastructure.

answer:
Both 10-Ks say scaling AI infrastructure is raising costs and pressuring margins — Microsoft describes it as already reducing its gross margin percentage, while Alphabet frames it as a forward-looking driver of significantly higher infrastructure costs and potential downward pressure on operating margin.

**Microsoft (FY2025 10-K, fiscal year ended June 30, 2025)**
- MD&A states that investments in cloud and AI infrastructure "will continue to increase our operating costs and may decrease our operating margins," with datacenter expansion dependent on land, energy, networking supplies, and servers including GPUs (p.34); the Risk Factors section similarly says it is "incurring significant costs to build and maintain infrastructure to support cloud-based and AI services, reducing operating margins" (p.17).
- In results, cost of revenue rose $13.7 billion or 19% driven by Microsoft Cloud, and gross margin percentage "decreased slightly"; Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage fell to 69% "driven by the impact of scaling our AI infrastructure, offset in part by efficiency gains in Azure" (p.37).
- The Intelligent Cloud segment shows the effect most clearly: cost of revenue up $10.6 billion or 36% driven by Azure, with gross margin percentage down from scaling AI infrastructure, partly offset by Azure efficiency gains (p.38).
- Database figures confirm this: cost of revenue grew 18.5% to $87.8 billion, gross margin percentage slipped from 69.8% to 68.8%, while operating margin actually rose from 44.6% to 45.6% on revenue growth of 15%.

**Alphabet (FY2025 10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025)**
- MD&A's "Increased Investment in Technical Infrastructure" trend says it invested heavily in capex in 2025 and expects to significantly increase investment in 2026 (servers, network equipment, data centers); operating costs of that infrastructure — depreciation, energy, equipment, and network capacity — "are expected to significantly increase" because AI offerings require more compute power than historical offerings, though it expects to keep driving efficiencies through AI model design and its TPU/GPU-based infrastructure (p.30).
- The same section warns that AI offerings (AI Overviews, AI Mode in Search, enterprise AI on Cloud) "may monetize differently" than historical offerings, which could affect revenue growth rates and margin trends (p.30).
- Risk Factors flag possible "downward pressure on our operating margin" from the higher level of technical infrastructure investment, noting some costs are relatively fixed and efficiencies may not continue at the past rate (p.12).
- Database figures show the pressure is prospective rather than realized: cost of revenue grew 11.1% to $162.5 billion, gross margin percentage actually improved from 58.2% to 59.7%, and operating margin was roughly flat (32.1% to 32.0%).

**The contrast:** Microsoft reports the margin impact as current — AI infrastructure scaling has already cut its gross margin percentage, especially in Microsoft Cloud (down to 69%) — whereas Alphabet reports stable-to-better margins in FY2025 and positions the cost and margin impact as an expected, significant increase going into 2026, mitigated by datacenter efficiencies.

Apple's FY2025 10-K (Item 1A) discloses two dedicated supply chain risk factors — dependence on outsourced manufacturing/logistics partners and the ability to obtain components in sufficient quantities — plus related trade-restriction and business-interruption risks that directly target its supply chain.

- **Dependence on outsourcing partners (p.10):** A significant majority of Apple's manufacturing is performed by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, with single-source partners in the U.S., Asia and Europe supplying many components and partners primarily in Asia performing final assembly of substantially all hardware products. Outsourcing lowers costs but reduces direct control over production and distribution, which has from time to time adversely affected cost, quality or quantity; Apple also generally remains responsible to consumers for warranty service on product defects, and supplier code of conduct violations occur from time to time. Changes or additions to the supply chain require considerable time and resources and carry additional regulatory and operational risks.

- **Component availability and pricing (pp.10–11):** Certain components come from single or limited sources, exposing Apple to significant supply and pricing risks, and even multi-source components face industry-wide shortages and commodity price fluctuations — the filing cites past global semiconductor shortages that impaired Apple's ability to obtain components on commercially reasonable terms. New products often use custom components available from only one source with initial capacity constraints, and Apple may be unable to extend or renew supply agreements, find alternative sources, or keep suppliers from failing, consolidating, or prioritizing common components over Apple's custom needs.

- **Trade restrictions and tariffs (p.8):** Restrictions on international trade — including the new U.S. tariffs announced beginning in the second quarter of 2025 on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU, threatened reciprocal tariffs, and a Section 232 investigation into semiconductor imports — can materially adversely affect Apple's supply chain by raising costs or limiting availability of products, components, rare earths and other raw materials, and could force supplier changes and restructuring that are expensive, time-consuming and disruptive. The filing notes global supply chains are highly concentrated and that escalation of geopolitical tensions or conflict could result in significant disruptions.

- **Business interruptions (p.8):** Political events, trade and international disputes, geopolitical tensions, conflict, terrorism, natural disasters, public health issues and industrial accidents can materially adversely affect Apple's suppliers, contract manufacturers and logistics providers.

- **Related margin and product-transition risks (pp.10, 17):** Supply shortages and potential increases in component and outside manufacturing costs are cited as sources of net sales and gross margin volatility, and new product transitions carry production ramp-up risks, purchase-commitment management and inventory-level risks.

answer:
Microsoft's FY2025 10-K discloses AI-related risks throughout Item 1A (Risk Factors), anchored by a dedicated risk factor titled "Issues in the development, deployment, and use of AI may result in reputational or competitive harm or liability." The main themes are:

- **Development and deployment flaws (p.23):** AI algorithms or training methodologies may be flawed; datasets may be overbroad, insufficient, or contain biased or inaccurate information; and AI-generated content may be offensive, illegal, inaccurate, or otherwise harmful. Inadequate practices by Microsoft or others (including strategic partner OpenAI) could cause incidents that impair acceptance of AI solutions, and human review may be required, including for agentic AI systems that act autonomously.
- **Legal, IP, and privacy exposure (pp.23, 27):** AI implementation could result in legal liability, regulatory action, or brand/reputational/competitive harm, stemming from intellectual property, data privacy, and other claims associated with AI training and outputs; third parties have made copyright infringement and other claims arising from AI training and output, which Microsoft may resolve via royalty-bearing licenses, product redesign, or damages.
- **Regulation (p.24):** Emerging AI legislation could increase costs or restrict opportunity — for example, the EU's AI Act may increase costs or impact provision/operation of AI models and services in Europe, with regulatory focus on model and system development and deployment, frontier model safety, transparency, and content provenance.
- **Competition and execution (p.17):** AI is a highly competitive, rapidly evolving market with new entrants; Microsoft will bear significant development and operational costs to build AI models, services, platforms, and infrastructure, and its cloud/AI infrastructure spending is reducing operating margins. Success depends on execution (compelling services, device compatibility, developer attractiveness, reliability/security), and it is uncertain whether strategies will generate revenue in line with these investments. Competitors also distribute open AI models at little or no cost without bearing full R&D costs.
- **Investment returns (p.18):** Significant investments in AI-based products and services are speculative — revenue may not materialize for several years, if at all, and margins may be below historical levels.
- **Misuse and abuse (pp.18, 22):** AI systems may be used in unintended or inappropriate ways, including fraudulent or abusive activity through cloud and AI services (unauthorized account access, payment fraud, cryptocurrency mining, launching cyberattacks); users may impersonate people or organizations through AI technologies; and customers may deploy Microsoft's AI products in high-risk scenarios or use them inappropriately, exposing Microsoft to legal claims or enforcement actions.
- **Security and reputation (pp.19–20, 27):** Threat actors may use AI and machine learning in attacks, generative AI in internal systems may create new attack surfaces, and generative AI features can be susceptible to security threats; reputational damage could also come from public scrutiny of AI decisions and responsible AI failures, and AI solutions with unintended consequences or contrary to responsible AI policies (impacting human rights, privacy, or employment) could hurt the business.

Apple's FY2025 10-K discloses two dedicated supply chain risk factors in Item 1A — dependence on outsourced manufacturing/logistics partners and obtaining components in sufficient quantities — plus related trade-restriction and business-interruption risks.

- **Outsourcing dependence (p.10):** Most manufacturing is done by partners in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, plus U.S. sourcing; single-source partners in the U.S., Asia and Europe; final assembly primarily in Asia; logistics outsourced.
- These arrangements reduce direct control over production and distribution, which has at times adversely affected cost, quality, quantity and flexibility.
- Apple remains responsible for warranty and out-of-warranty service despite defect-reimbursement provisions; supplier code of conduct violations occur and can materially adversely affect the business.
- Supply chain changes or additions require considerable time and resources and carry regulatory and operational risks.
- **Component availability (pp.10–11):** Certain components are single- or limited-source; even multi-source components face industry-wide shortages and commodity price fluctuations — past global semiconductor shortages cited as an example that could recur.
- New products use custom components from only one source, with initial capacity constraints until yields mature; supply agreements may not be extended or renewed on similar terms, or at all.
- Suppliers may fail, consolidate, or shift to common components instead of Apple-customized ones, causing shortages and price increases.
- **Trade restrictions and tariffs (p.8):** Beginning Q2 2025, new U.S. tariffs on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the EU; retaliatory measures threatened; Section 232 semiconductor import investigation underway; measures may raise costs, limit availability of products, components, rare earths and raw materials, and force supplier and operational changes.
- Global supply chains are highly concentrated; escalating geopolitical tensions or conflict could cause significant disruptions.
- **Business interruptions (p.8):** Political events, trade disputes, geopolitical tensions, conflict, terrorism, natural disasters, public health issues and industrial accidents can affect suppliers, contract manufacturers and logistics providers.
- **Margin pressure (p.17):** Supply shortages and potential increases in component and outside manufacturing services costs are among factors pressuring net sales and gross margins.

Microsoft's FY2025 10-K discloses AI risks in a dedicated risk factor on AI development, deployment, and use, plus AI mentions in its competition, execution, security, IP, regulatory, and reputation risk factors.

- **Development/deployment flaws (p.23):** Flawed AI algorithms or training methodologies; datasets overbroad, insufficient, or containing biased or inaccurate information; AI-generated content may be offensive, illegal, inaccurate, or harmful.
- **Partner practices (p.23):** Inadequate practices by Microsoft or others, including strategic partner OpenAI, could cause incidents impairing AI acceptance or harming individuals, customers, or society; human review of inputs/outputs may be required, including for autonomous agentic AI.
- **Claims and regulation (p.23):** IP, data privacy, and other claims tied to AI training and outputs; evolving regulatory landscape including new EU laws, ethical issues, and global divergence.
- **Competition (p.17):** AI is a highly competitive, rapidly evolving market with new entrants; competitors distribute open AI models at little or no cost without full R&D costs.
- **Execution costs (p.17):** Significant development, operational, and infrastructure costs for AI models, services, platforms, and infrastructure are reducing operating margins; uncertain whether strategies will attract users or generate matching revenue.
- **Misuse (pp.18, 22):** AI used in unintended or inappropriate ways; fraudulent or abusive activities via cloud and AI services (unauthorized account access, payment fraud, cryptocurrency mining, cyberattacks); detection may not be effective.
- **Impersonation (p.22):** Users may impersonate people or organizations through AI technologies and disseminate misleading content.
- **Investment returns (p.18):** AI investments are speculative, may not be profitable, and may not achieve historical operating margins.
- **Security (pp.19–20):** Threat actors may use AI/ML in attacks; generative AI in internal systems may create new attack surfaces; generative AI features can be susceptible to security threats.
- **Customer deployment (p.22):** Customers control AI products in their environments and may deploy them in high-risk scenarios; products may collect data in ways not satisfying customer or regulatory requirements, risking claims or enforcement.
- **IP (p.27):** Third-party infringement claims, including current copyright claims arising from AI training and output, could force royalty-bearing data access, licensing, product redesigns, or indemnification damages.
- **Regulation (p.24):** Emerging AI legislation could increase costs or restrict opportunity; the EU AI Act may impact AI models and services in the European market; areas include frontier model safety, transparency, and content provenance.
- **Reputation (p.27):** Public scrutiny of AI development and deployment decisions and responsible AI failures could damage Microsoft's brands and reputation.
